name: Cheerleader Effect
description: A person can look more attractive when seen as part of a group than when seen alone. Group context shifts perception of the individual, not just the group.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to avatars, team photos, creator cards, dating/social products, testimonial layouts, and any interface that alternates between solo portraits and grouped presentation. Presentation context can change person-level impression.
prevalence_note: Mostly a niche popular-psychology/social-media term with occasional relevance to profile-photo or group-shot design, not a standard concept in mainstream UX canon.

findings.description: Across five experiments, the same face was rated as more attractive when shown in a same-gender group than when shown alone. Walker and Vul proposed that ensemble averaging within the group shifts the perceived individual toward a more attractive average.
findings.source_title: Hierarchical Encoding Makes Individuals in a Group Seem More Attractive

findings.description: Two direct replications of Walker and Vul's key experiment again found that individuals presented in a group are judged more attractive than the same individuals shown alone, corroborating the cheerleader effect on the original paradigm.
findings.source_title: Two replications of "Hierarchical encoding makes individuals in a group seem more attractive (2014; Experiment 4)".
